title: State v. Payne
description: Whether a trial court has jurisdiction to reconsider the consecutive alignment of a defendant's original sentences after a determination of intellectual disability under Tennessee Code Annotated section 39-13-203(g).
plaintiff_argument: Payne argued that the trial court retained broad discretion over sentencing matters, including sentence alignment, after his intellectual disability determination, and no statute expressly forbade it.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the trial court lacked jurisdiction to realign sentences because once a criminal judgment is final, it cannot be modified unless a statute or rule authorizes it, and no such authorization existed for sentence realignment in this context.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's modification of Payne's two death sentences to sentences of life imprisonment but vacated the trial court's realignment of Payne's sentences, finding it lacked jurisdiction to modify the judgment in that respect.

title: Wygant v. Lee (formerly Moore v. Lee)
description: Whether a voter has standing to challenge the constitutionality of her own voting district due to alleged representational harm, with the plaintiff arguing she has standing due to representational harm from misnumbering and a 3-1 staggered-term system, and the defendant arguing she lacks standing as her injury is not particularized or imminent.
plaintiff_argument: Ms. Hunt argues she has standing to challenge the constitutionality of her voting district because she suffered representational harm from being placed in an unconstitutionally configured district, including a 3-1 staggered-term representative structure.
defendant_argument: The majority (defendant's side) concluded that Ms. Hunt lacked standing, asserting her alleged injury was conjectural, hypothetical, or a mere possibility, and not a particularized injury.
decision_outcome: The court's majority ruled that Ms. Hunt lacked standing to challenge the constitutionality of her voting district.

title: State v. Green
description: Whether a drug-sniffing canine's positive alert, despite its inability to distinguish between legal hemp and illegal marijuana, can still contribute to probable cause for a vehicle search under the totality of the circumstances.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that a positive alert from a certified drug-detection dog, even with hemp legalization, still establishes probable cause, or at least contributes to it under a totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that a canine sniff cannot provide probable cause because the dog cannot differentiate between legal hemp and illegal marijuana, making any alert unreliable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Criminal Appeals' judgment, ruling that law enforcement possessed probable cause to search the vehicle and reinstating the indictments against the defendant.

title: McKay v. State
description: Whether Public Chapter 182 violates Article VI, § 5 of the Tennessee Constitution by transferring representation of the State in capital collateral review proceedings from the locally elected district attorney to the Attorney General.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Larry McKay, argued that Public Chapter 182 violates Article VI, § 5 of the Tennessee Constitution by unconstitutionally transferring the authority to represent the State in capital collateral review proceedings from the locally elected district attorney to the Attorney General, thereby impeding the inherent discretion and authority of the district attorney.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Tennessee (represented by the Attorney General), argued that Public Chapter 182 is constitutional because Article VI, § 5 does not grant exclusive control to district attorneys over collateral review proceedings, which are quasi-civil and not criminal prosecutions, and the legislature has the authority to define the duties of the district attorney.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's order, finding Public Chapter 182 constitutional and that it does not violate Article VI, § 5 of the Tennessee Constitution.

title: Smith v. BlueCross BlueShield of Tennessee
description: Whether the constitutional right to petition in the Tennessee Constitution applies to private employers as a public policy exception to the employment-at-will doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that her termination for emailing legislators about vaccine mandates violated Tennessee's public policy, based on her constitutional right to petition, which should be an exception to at-will employment.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the termination was lawful under the employment-at-will doctrine because the right to petition only protects against government action, not private employers, and thus does not create a public policy exception.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Court of Appeals, affirming the trial court's dismissal, holding that the right to petition in the Tennessee Constitution is enforceable only against governmental entities and not private parties, and therefore cannot be a basis for a public policy exception to at-will employment against private employers.

title: Rainwaters v. Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency
description: Whether Tennessee Code Annotated subsections 70-1-305(1) and (7), which authorize warrantless and non-consensual entry onto private property by TWRA officers, are constitutional both facially and as applied.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the statute authorizing warrantless entries onto private property is unconstitutional on its face and as applied, violating their rights under Article I, Section 7 of the Tennessee Constitution, and sought declaratory and injunctive relief as well as nominal damages.
defendant_argument: The defendant, TWRA, argued that the statute is facially constitutional and constitutional as applied, asserting its officers have lawful authority to enter private property without a warrant or consent to enforce wildlife laws, and that the plaintiffs' properties are not constitutionally protected.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the statute is facially constitutional but unconstitutional as applied to the plaintiffs, and affirmed the award of nominal damages.

title: Dotson v. State
description: Whether the provisions of Tennessee Supreme Court Rule 13 for prior approval review of expert funding requests are constitutional as applied, whether the Petitioner was unconstitutionally denied appellate review of the denial of expert funds, and whether the Petitioner was deprived of a full and fair post-conviction hearing due to the denial of expert funds.
plaintiff_argument: The Petitioner argued that Rule 13's prior approval provisions are unconstitutional, that he was unconstitutionally denied appellate review of expert funds, and that he was deprived of a full and fair post-conviction hearing due to the denial of expert funds.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Rule 13 provisions are constitutional, the Petitioner was not unconstitutionally denied appellate review, and he received a full and fair post-conviction hearing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgments of the post-conviction court and the Court of Criminal Appeals, holding that Rule 13 provisions are constitutional, the Petitioner was not unconstitutionally denied appellate review, and he received a full and fair post-conviction hearing.

title: Falls v. Goins
description: Whether Ernest Falls' right to vote in Tennessee was automatically restored upon receiving clemency in Virginia, or if he must also comply with additional Tennessee statutory requirements for re-enfranchisement.
plaintiff_argument: Ernest Falls argued that his right to vote in Tennessee was automatically restored when Virginia granted him clemency, as per Tennessee Code Annotated section 2-19-143(3).
defendant_argument: The State Officials argued that Mr. Falls must comply with additional requirements under Tennessee Code Annotated section 40-29-202, such as paying court costs, restitution, and child support, to regain his voting rights.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, ruling that Ernest Falls must comply with both Tennessee Code Annotated sections 2-19-143(3) and 40-29-202 to regain his right to vote in Tennessee.

title: Metropolitan Government of Nashville & Davidson County v. Tennessee Department of Education
description: Whether the Education Savings Account Pilot Program (ESA Act) violates the Home Rule Amendment of the Tennessee Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The ESA Act violates the Home Rule Amendment because it is local in form or effect, applicable to the counties in their governmental capacity, and does not require local approval, thereby infringing on local control of local affairs and requiring them to fund LEAs at the same level despite students leaving for private schools.
defendant_argument: The ESA Act does not violate the Home Rule Amendment because it only regulates Local Education Agencies (LEAs), which are distinct from county governments, and therefore is not 'applicable to' the counties themselves in the meaning of the Home Rule Amendment.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals' judgment, holding that the ESA Act does not implicate the Home Rule Amendment and is therefore not unconstitutional on that basis, remanding the case for dismissal of that claim.
